result:
Strangler fig pattern: wrap the monolith with a router (API gateway or facade), peel off bounded domains one at a time, redirect their traffic through the new service. Data stays in the monolith until a service owns its slice; backfill happens async or on-demand.

**Ordering:** Extract services in dependency order (bottom-up). Start with leaf domains that nothing else depends on—reporting, notifications, audit logs—so they don't block other extractions. High-fan-in domains (auth, core entity lookups) come last because everything talks to them; moving them is risky until most other services are ready.

**Data ownership:** Dual-write during transition. New service writes its own tables; the monolith still owns the source-of-truth copy for reads until traffic fully switches. Use event log or change data capture to sync writes back to monolith (or forward to service, depending on direction). Once traffic 100% routes to the service, drop the dual-write, make monolith copy eventually consistent or archive it. Don't flip ownership all at once—gradually move reads too.

**Shippable continuously:** Each service ships independently, routes through the gateway (feature-flagged or percentage-based), old code stays dormant but deployed. If the new service fails, traffic bounces back to monolith code without rollback. Version the service contracts and test both old and new paths before flipping percentage. Keep monolith and service in sync for a sprint or two—don't let them diverge enough that rollback breaks.

**Gotchas:** Transactions and consistency. The monolith had ACID; services don't. Identify places that need it (payment, reservations) and either keep those in monolith longer, use saga patterns, or accept eventual consistency earlier than you think. Cross-domain queries slow down—cache aggressively or denormalize into read models.

**Win condition:** When monolith has no business logic left (just CRUD behind a gateway), you can rewrite or retire it.
